title: M5 Ultra and 512GB Mac Studio
hook: Apple's new Mac Studio pairs M5 Max and M5 Ultra with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth — the desktop that can hold a frontier-size model in RAM.
key_points: Apple introduced a Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, configurable up to 512GB of unified memory.
The M5 Ultra is reported at 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth.
Unified memory means the GPU addresses all of it, so model size is bounded by RAM rather than by a discrete card's VRAM.
For local inference, bandwidth is the usual limit on tokens per second once the weights fit.
The local-LLM community reads this as a workstation that can run very large open-weight models without a multi-GPU rig.
content_html: Apple introduced a new Mac Studio built around the M5 Max and M5 Ultra, configurable to 512GB of unified memory, with the M5 Ultra reported at 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. It is a consumer product launch, but the local-model community treated it as an inference hardware announcement.
extra_html:
Why the local-LLM crowd cares

Two numbers decide whether a machine can run a big open-weight model: how much memory the accelerator can address, and how fast it can read it. Apple's unified memory architecture collapses the first question into "how much RAM did you buy," which is how a desktop ends up with more usable model capacity than a stack of discrete GPUs. The second number sets the ceiling on speed, since decoding streams the weights once per token — hence the attention paid to 1.2 TB/s.

Discussion on r/LocalLLaMA speculated about the memory technology involved and what a future generation might reach; those are community guesses, not Apple specifications. The durable point is the shape of the trade: high-capacity, high-bandwidth unified memory makes single-box local inference of very large models a normal thing to attempt.

flashcards.prompt: Why does unified memory matter for running large models locally?
flashcards.back_html: The GPU addresses the whole pool, so what fits is bounded by system RAM — up to 512GB here — instead of a discrete card's much smaller VRAM.

flashcards.prompt: Once a model's weights fit in memory, what usually limits local generation speed?
flashcards.explanation_html: Autoregressive decoding streams the weights for every token, so tokens per second tracks bandwidth — which is why the M5 Ultra's reported 1.2 TB/s is the number the local-LLM community fixated on.
